sections.title: Recognising the egg stage
sections.text: A young amanita is entirely enclosed in a smooth, thick, white universal veil. A lengthwise cut may reveal a formed stem, gills and cap inside; a puffball remains uniformly white and homogeneous. The cut shows an amanita egg but cannot identify the species by itself.

sections.title: Development
sections.text: As it grows, the veil splits, leaving a ring on the stem and a sac-like volva at the base. In Amanita phalloides the cap may become greenish, yellow-green or olive, though young specimens are often nearly white.

sections.title: Lookalike and safety
sections.text: Amanita eggs can be mistaken for puffballs. A death cap is already dangerous at this stage: amatoxins resist cooking and a small amount can cause severe poisoning. Possible ingestion requires an immediate call to emergency services or a poison centre; do not wait for symptoms.

sections.title: Symptom delay
sections.text: Digestive symptoms often begin after several hours, commonly around 6–24 hours and sometimes as late as 48 hours. The liver is mainly affected; the kidneys can also be injured.

traits: When young, a white egg wrapped in the universal veil
Smooth surface, no spines or warts
A lengthwise cut reveals a formed young mushroom inside the veil, but does not identify the species by itself
As it grows: ring and sac-like volva; the death-cap can become greenish, though young caps are often pale
Can be mistaken for a uniformly white puffball; do not eat
safetyNote: A death cap may already be deadly at the egg stage. Amatoxins resist cooking; symptoms can appear 6–48 hours after ingestion, mainly affecting the liver. If ingestion is possible, call emergency services or a poison centre immediately and do not rely on a simple cut for identification.
